title: Targeted Protein Degradation: PROTACs & Glues
summary: Drugs that make cells destroy a target protein.

lessons.title: The ubiquitin–proteasome system

levels.kid:
Your cells have a cleanup crew. Old or damaged proteins get a tiny label, like a sticky note that says "throw this away." The label is called **ubiquitin**. A special machine called the **proteasome** reads the label, pulls the protein apart, and chops it into little pieces that can be reused.

Some proteins cause disease when there are too many of them or they won't switch off. Scientists wondered: what if a medicine could put the cleanup label on the troublesome protein? Then the cell would remove the whole protein instead of just blocking it. That idea leads to medicines called **protein degraders**. They borrow the cell's own cleanup machinery. But they must label the right protein—sending the wrong one for cleanup could be harmful.
levels.hs:
Cells constantly make and destroy proteins. One major disposal pathway is the **ubiquitin–proteasome system** (UPS).

The small protein **ubiquitin** is attached to a protein marked for destruction. Ubiquitin tagging involves three enzyme classes: **E1** activates ubiquitin, **E2** carries it, and an **E3 ligase** recognizes the target and transfers or helps transfer ubiquitin onto it. Repeated tagging builds a **polyubiquitin chain**. Chains linked through lysine 48 on ubiquitin are a classic signal for destruction.

The **26S proteasome** recognizes the chain, removes and recycles ubiquitin, unfolds the tagged protein, and feeds it into a barrel-shaped core that cuts it into short peptides. The cell can reuse the building blocks. **Deubiquitinases** can remove ubiquitin and rescue or edit tagged proteins.

Drug designers exploit this system to remove disease-associated proteins. If a small molecule brings a target protein next to an E3 ligase, the ligase can tag it, and the proteasome destroys it. Unlike an inhibitor that merely blocks an active site, degradation removes all of the protein's functions, including scaffold roles.

Not all ubiquitin chains mean disposal. Different chain linkages can signal DNA repair or cell signaling. And not every protein is easily degradable: it needs an accessible region for ubiquitination and initiation of proteasomal unfolding.
levels.college:
The ubiquitin–proteasome system provides regulated intracellular protein turnover. Ubiquitin, a 76-residue protein, is activated by E1 in an ATP-dependent step, transferred via a thioester to an E2, then attached to a substrate lysine (or sometimes other sites) by an E3 ligase. RING E3 ligases position E2 and substrate for direct transfer; HECT and RBR ligases form transient E3–ubiquitin intermediates.

Repeated ubiquitination forms polyubiquitin chains with different topologies. **K48-linked** chains are canonical proteasomal degradation signals; K63-linked chains often support signaling, trafficking and DNA repair, though biological outcomes depend on context. The 26S proteasome has a **20S catalytic core** and one or two **19S regulatory caps**. The 19S cap recognizes chains, uses ATPase subunits to unfold substrates, removes ubiquitin, and translocates polypeptides into the 20S core for cleavage.

Deubiquitinases (DUBs) trim or remove chains, offering quality control and regulatory checkpoints. Protein abundance reflects both synthesis and destruction; a drug that changes one cannot be assessed solely from an endpoint western blot.

For targeted degradation, pharmacological proximity recruits an E3 ligase to a protein of interest. This can strip catalytic and noncatalytic functions together. An ideal substrate has accessible surface lysines and an unstructured region that the proteasome can engage for unfolding, though sites and initiation rules vary.

Important controls: proteasome inhibitors should rescue target loss if degradation is UPS-dependent; E1 inhibition or ligase knockout should also interrupt the mechanism. Proteomics checks whether other proteins fall unexpectedly. A decrease in protein level by itself does not prove targeted degradation; transcriptional repression or cell toxicity can do the same.
levels.phd:
The UPS is a network, not a linear trash chute. Two human E1 enzymes activate ubiquitin; dozens of E2s and hundreds of E3 ligases create substrate specificity. E3 architecture matters: RING ligases recruit charged E2 for direct transfer, while HECT/RBR ligases form catalytic ubiquitin intermediates. E3 substrate receptors often sit in multisubunit complexes—cereblon in CRL4^CRBN and VHL in CRL2^VHL are widely used by degraders.

Polyubiquitin chains encode a rich signal. K48-linked chains classically route substrates to proteasomes; K63 supports signaling; K11 and mixed or branched chains also contribute to degradation. Chain length, topology and DUB editing affect recognition by proteasomal ubiquitin receptors such as Rpn10/Rpn13. The 19S ATPase ring unfolds substrates and commits them to 20S proteolysis, while associated DUBs recycle ubiquitin.

Physical substrate requirements matter for induced degradation. An E3 brought close to a target may still fail if lysines are badly oriented, if the E2 cannot reach them, or if the target lacks an accessible initiation region for unfolding. Ubiquitination and degradation are therefore distinct endpoints; measuring both helps diagnose failure.

Protein steady state follows d[P]/dt = synthesis − degradation. For a degrader, maximal extent and rate of depletion depend on synthesis, baseline half-life, E3 abundance, proteasome capacity and cell type. A tumor might express an E3 weakly and resist an otherwise potent degrader. Resistance can also arise from mutation or downregulation of the E3-complex machinery.

Controls include proteasome rescue, E1 inhibition, E3 loss-of-function, time-course ubiquitination, transcript measurements and global proteomics. Because proteasome inhibitors perturb many cellular systems, rescue by itself supports but does not uniquely prove a proposed E3 mechanism.
levels.expert:
A working degrader team starts by asking whether the biological goal requires removing the protein rather than inhibiting it. Kinase targets can have scaffold functions that persist under a catalytic inhibitor; degradation removes both. Conversely, removing the entire protein may cause broader biology than expected, so the gain must justify the risk.

First, map target expression and half-life across disease and healthy tissues. Check which E3 ligases are present and accessible in the intended cells. Cereblon and VHL are common workhorses, but their expression is not universal and their native biology can complicate selectivity. A target with rapid synthesis may need continuous degradation pressure; one with slow turnover may remain suppressed longer.

To interpret a depletion assay, show that RNA is not simply downregulated, cell viability is not globally collapsing, and the target's ubiquitination precedes its loss. Rescue with a proteasome inhibitor, disruption of E1 and genetic loss of the recruited E3 together build a causal chain. Quantitative proteomics then identifies other depleted proteins that could drive toxicities or even desired effects.

A senior chemist distinguishes **engagement**, **ubiquitination**, **degradation** and **functional response**. Binding both partners does not guarantee productive ubiquitination; ubiquitination does not guarantee proteasomal access; protein loss does not guarantee a useful phenotype. Each transition must be measured. Finally, monitor rebound after compound washout: protein resynthesis and tissue-specific turnover determine how often sustained intervention would be needed, not the drug's plasma curve alone.

keyPoints: E1 activates ubiquitin, E2 carries it, and E3 selects substrates.
K48-linked chains classically direct proteins to the 26S proteasome.
The 19S cap recognizes and unfolds; the 20S core cleaves.
DUBs remove or edit ubiquitin chains; not every chain signals destruction.
Binding, ubiquitination, degradation and functional response are distinct steps.

lessons.title: PROTAC architecture

levels.kid:
A **PROTAC** is a molecule with two grabbing ends joined by a chain. One end holds a protein that scientists want to remove. The other end holds the cell's labeling helper, called an **E3 ligase**. When both ends grab at once, the helper can put a ubiquitin cleanup label on the target. Then the cell's proteasome breaks that target down.

The clever part is that the PROTAC often lets go afterward. It can help label another target, like a teacher handing out more than one name tag. But its two-ended shape makes it bigger than many ordinary medicines, and big molecules can have trouble getting inside cells. Scientists change the chain and the grabbing ends to solve that problem.
levels.hs:
**PROTAC** stands for PROteolysis-TArgeting Chimera. It's a two-headed molecule built from three parts:
1. A **target-binding ligand**, which grabs the protein of interest.
2. An **E3-ligase ligand**, which recruits a cell's ubiquitin-labeling machinery, commonly cereblon (CRBN) or VHL.
3. A **linker** joining the two ligands.

When the PROTAC binds both proteins, it forms a **ternary complex**: target–PROTAC–E3. The E3 can attach ubiquitin to the target. A polyubiquitin chain signals the proteasome to break it down. The PROTAC can then be released and recruit another target, giving it **event-driven** rather than occupancy-driven action: it does not need to sit on the target continuously to keep it blocked.

A traditional inhibitor must occupy enough copies of a protein to block its activity. A PROTAC can sometimes work even with a weak target-binding ligand because repeated degradation removes target molecules. But it's not guaranteed to recycle: some molecules become trapped or are cleared quickly.

Design challenges include the large size and many polar groups of PROTACs, which can make cell entry and oral absorption difficult. The **linker's length and flexibility** matter enormously: too short or too long can position the E3 incorrectly. Chemists test linker series and use structural studies to find productive geometry.
levels.college:
A PROTAC comprises a ligand for the protein of interest (POI), a ligand for an E3 ligase substrate receptor, and a linker. Common E3 recruiters are CRBN (within CRL4^CRBN) and VHL (within CRL2^VHL), though hundreds of E3s offer untapped possibilities. Binding each partner brings them into a ternary complex; E2/E3 machinery transfers ubiquitin to accessible POI lysines, and polyubiquitinated POI may undergo proteasomal degradation.

This is **event-driven pharmacology**: a single molecule may catalyze multiple rounds of degradation after release. Target occupancy need not be maintained continuously. Degradation metrics differ from inhibitor IC50: **DC50** is concentration yielding half-maximal degradation at a defined time, and **Dmax** is the maximal fraction depleted. Both vary with time and cell type.

The linker is not an inert spacer. Length, rigidity, hydrophobicity and exit-vector geometry determine ternary-complex formation and productive ubiquitination. PEG linkers increase solubility but can increase polarity; alkyl and constrained linkers may improve permeability. Intramolecular folding can hide polar surface and aid cell entry despite high nominal polar surface area.

PROTACs often exceed Lipinski Rule-of-Five guidelines (high molecular weight and H-bond counts). That does not prohibit activity, but permeability, efflux and oral exposure require special attention. Off-targets can arise from either ligand binding other proteins or from neosubstrate recruitment by the E3 ligand itself. Controls include separate ligands, an E3-binding-deficient stereoisomer, genetic E3 disruption and proteasome inhibition.

Several PROTAC candidates have reached clinical testing, especially targeting androgen receptor, estrogen receptor and BTK; clinical status evolves, so discovery claims should distinguish trials from approved drugs.
levels.phd:
PROTAC design is an optimization problem in induced protein proximity, not simply a matter of linking two high-affinity ligands. The productive ternary complex has geometry permitting E2-to-substrate lysine transfer. Structural complementarity between target and E3 surfaces creates **cooperativity**: positive cooperativity stabilizes the ternary complex beyond the sum of binary interactions; negative cooperativity destabilizes it. Linker exit vectors and conformational ensembles govern this protein–protein interface.

Event-driven action can confer substoichiometric degradation, but catalytic turnover has limits. A degrader tightly trapped in a ternary complex, sequestered in membranes, or rapidly metabolized may not recycle efficiently. Rate-limiting steps can move from ternary assembly to ubiquitin transfer, proteasomal unfolding or resynthesis. DC50 and Dmax are operational descriptors measured at specified times; they are not equilibrium affinity constants.

Chemical biology controls distinguish induced degradation from inhibition. A nondegrading stereochemical control that still binds the target isolates degradation-specific effects; E3 knockout and proteasome inhibition test pathway dependence. Proteome-wide mass spectrometry measures selectivity and can expose novel neosubstrates created by the E3-recruiting moiety.

Beyond-Rule-of-Five (bRo5) physicochemistry is central. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds and conformational collapse lower exposed polarity in membranes (the "chameleonicity" concept). PAMPA and Caco-2 permeability alone can mislead when transporters, efflux or intracellular sequestration matter. CRBN- and VHL-binding motifs also present different metabolic and synthetic liabilities. New ligases may provide tissue selectivity or alter resistance pathways, but their ligand chemistry and safety are less mature.

Future design combines ternary-complex structural data, cellular ubiquitinomics and quantitative PK/PD models to optimize not just binding, but how fast a disease-relevant protein disappears in the right tissue.
levels.expert:
The design meeting starts with a target rationale: is the protein's noncatalytic function worth removing, and can a small molecule bind it at all? A weak ligand may suffice for a degrader, but it must engage the protein in cells.

Build a matrix of target binders, E3 recruiters and linker lengths/exit vectors. For each compound measure cellular target engagement, E3 engagement, ternary-complex formation, ubiquitination, DC50, Dmax and time course of target loss. A single Western blot after one incubation tells too little. Negative controls include a stereoisomer that loses E3 binding, a ligand lacking the degrader linker, proteasome blockade and E3 knockout.

A medicinal chemist learns to separate three failure types: (1) compound never enters cells; (2) both partners are bound but geometry doesn't permit ubiquitination; (3) the target is tagged but resynthesis or poor proteasomal initiation prevents deep depletion. Each requires a different fix. Linker length and rigidity are not cosmetic. Don't chase ternary affinity alone at the expense of productive ubiquitination.

Large size and polarity create difficult exposure problems. Measure passive permeability and efflux; check solubility, microsomal stability, plasma binding and tissue distribution. An in-vitro degrader with excellent DC50 may not reach its target organ. Tissue-specific E3 expression can make a seemingly potent molecule inactive in the disease tissue.

Finally, distinguish clinical candidates from approved therapies. Clinical trials establish safety and efficacy only after they report, not because a compound entered a trial. The honest project slide shows mechanistic evidence and the remaining exposure and selectivity liabilities side by side.

keyPoints: PROTAC = target ligand + linker + E3 ligase recruiter.
Ternary target–PROTAC–E3 complex enables ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction.
Event-driven action may permit repeated target degradation.
Linker geometry and cooperativity matter beyond binary affinity.
DC50 and Dmax depend on assay time; size and polarity challenge exposure.

lessons.title: Ternary complexes & the hook effect

levels.kid: A PROTAC must hold two proteins at once. Imagine using both hands to bring two friends together. If you have too few PROTAC molecules, not many pairs meet. But strangely, having way too many can also be bad: each friend grabs a *different* PROTAC, so they don't meet each other! Scientists call that the **hook effect**. A good medicine needs enough pairs where one PROTAC holds both proteins. The pair's shape matters too: even if the friends meet, the labeling helper must be in the right position to put a cleanup tag on the target. More grabbing power is not always better.
levels.hs:
A PROTAC works only when it creates a productive **ternary complex**: protein of interest (POI), PROTAC and E3 ligase together. Binding each partner separately does not guarantee success. The E3 must be positioned so its ubiquitin-transfer machinery can reach a suitable site on the target.

At low PROTAC concentration, few ternary complexes form, so degradation is weak. At intermediate concentration, productive complexes form often and degradation rises. At very high concentration, each protein can bind a separate PROTAC molecule; target–PROTAC and PROTAC–E3 binary complexes compete with target–PROTAC–E3 ternary complexes. Degradation may fall. This bell-shaped response is the **hook effect** (also called a prozone effect).

The hook effect is not guaranteed for every degrader. Its size depends on the strength of each binary interaction, ternary cooperativity and assay conditions. **Positive cooperativity** means the target and E3 interact favorably when brought together, stabilizing the ternary complex and often reducing the hook effect. Negative cooperativity has the opposite tendency.

To test a PROTAC, scientists measure a wide concentration range, not just the rising part. They examine ternary complex formation, target ubiquitination, and actual target loss. Seeing a hook tells you that a higher concentration may work worse, but it doesn't tell you whether the compound is safe or effective in the body.
levels.college:
Ternary-complex thermodynamics govern PROTAC pharmacology. Each PROTAC forms binary complexes with the POI and E3 ligase; productive degradation requires the ternary POI–PROTAC–E3 assembly in a geometry supporting lysine ubiquitination. **Cooperativity α** describes how binding one partner changes affinity for the other: α > 1 positive, α < 1 negative, in a common convention.

At increasing degrader concentrations, ternary complex generally rises, peaks and may decline because separate binary complexes dominate when excess free PROTAC saturates both proteins. This is the **hook effect**; the degree of decline depends on binding constants, α and cellular conditions. Not every cellular concentration–degradation curve displays an obvious hook: permeability, E3 levels, assay time and target resynthesis can mask it.

Geometry. Structural studies of ternary complexes show that favorable target–E3 contacts can create strong positive cooperativity even if each binary ligand binds only modestly. The linker determines orientation and can turn a nondegrading pair of ligands into a potent degrader, or vice versa. Protein surface complementarity affects selectivity: a PROTAC with a promiscuous target ligand may nevertheless degrade only proteins whose surfaces form productive E3 complexes.

Measurement. TR-FRET, AlphaLISA, SPR or native MS can probe ternary formation; ubiquitin-remnant profiling and immunoblot/proteomics measure downstream effects. Compare ternary formation with degradation across dose and time. A strong ternary signal with no ubiquitination suggests unproductive geometry or inaccessible lysines. Ubiquitination without depletion points toward proteasome engagement, unfolding or high synthesis rate.

The clinical lesson: do not assume "more compound = more effect" for bifunctional agents; characterize the entire concentration–response curve.
levels.phd:
The hook effect follows from mass-action equilibria for a three-component system. At intermediate PROTAC concentration, both target and ligase occupy the same molecule; in large excess, each partner becomes sequestered into separate binary complexes. The exact location and magnitude of the peak depend on binary dissociation constants, target/E3 abundances and cooperativity α. A highly positive α stabilizes ternary assembly and can shift or attenuate the hook, but kinetics, target depletion and intracellular compound partitioning complicate equilibrium predictions.

Structural cooperativity is a design lever. For example, crystal structures of ternary complexes can reveal new target–ligase interfaces stabilized by a linker-specific conformation. A change in linker stereochemistry may preserve binary binding while disrupting this interface, sharply changing degradation. Such data explain why inhibitor affinity correlates imperfectly with degrader potency.

Cellular assays convolve ternary equilibrium with time-dependent pharmacology: ubiquitin transfer, proteasomal commitment, target resynthesis, E3 auto-ubiquitination and compound transport. A dose–response without a visible hook does not disprove the mechanism; cellular free concentration may never reach the regime that saturates both partners. Conversely, a declining high-concentration response can reflect toxicity or assay interference instead of a true hook, so orthogonal ternary and viability measurements are necessary.

Quantitative approaches fit mechanistic models to multiplexed observations: cellular target engagement for both ends, ternary formation, ubiquitination rate and depletion versus time. Ligase knockout and rescue help attribute the signal. Quantifying intracellular unbound compound rather than nominal media concentration greatly improves interpretation because PROTACs can be highly bound or effluxed.

For medicinal chemistry, optimize **productive ternary complex abundance and ubiquitin transfer**, not isolated binary affinity. The best binder is not necessarily the best degrader, and the best biochemical degrader may lack cellular exposure.
levels.expert:
A practical degrader screen starts with a broad concentration series and at least two time points. Too many campaigns stop at the first strong DC50 and miss a high-concentration downturn that matters for exposure decisions.

When a hook appears, don't simply label it a liability. Ask whether the decline occurs at intracellular concentrations attainable in the intended tissue. Model binary affinities, relative protein abundances and ternary cooperativity. An overly tight E3 ligand may saturate ligase as isolated binary complex; linker optimization can favor the productive interface without weakening needed target engagement.

Disentangle stages experimentally. Measure engagement of target and E3 separately, then ternary formation, target ubiquitination, and depletion. A reporter assay for ternary proximity can be misleading if it detects closeness but not correct E2 positioning; orthogonal structural or ubiquitination data matter. Compare proteomics at high concentration to see whether off-target depletion emerges as nominal on-target effect drops.

Common diagnostic branches:
- No ternary complex: adjust binding groups or linker length.
- Ternary complex without ubiquitination: change exit vector, linker rigidity or E3 recruiter to expose target lysines.
- Ubiquitination without loss: test proteasomal initiation and target turnover.
- Strong biochemical but weak cellular response: investigate permeability, efflux and intracellular sequestration.
- Downturn only in one readout: check assay saturation, interference and viability before invoking a hook.

The senior team's conclusion should describe the achievable window of cellular free concentration and measured target loss, not just a slogan about the hook effect. The goal is a robust degradation profile at plausible exposure.

keyPoints: A productive ternary complex brings target and E3 into ubiquitination geometry.
Excess degrader can sequester partners in separate binary complexes: hook effect.
Positive cooperativity stabilizes ternary complexes.
Not all degrader curves show a visible hook, and downturns can have other causes.
Measure engagement, ternary formation, ubiquitination and depletion separately.

lessons.title: Molecular glues (IMiDs)

levels.kid:
A PROTAC has two ends joined by a chain. A **molecular glue** does a similar job with just one small molecule. Imagine a drop of glue placed where two puzzle pieces nearly fit. The glue makes the pieces stick together: a troublesome protein and the E3 labeling helper. The helper tags the protein with ubiquitin, and the cell's cleanup machine removes it.

Some medicines called **IMiDs** work in part this way. They stick to an E3 helper named **cereblon** and change which proteins that helper grabs. Scientists were surprised to learn that a small medicine could change a cell's "remove this protein" list. But these glues must be carefully checked: one tiny change to the medicine can make it remove a different protein.
levels.hs:
**Molecular glues** are small molecules that cause two proteins to stick together or strengthen a weak contact. Some glues bring a target protein to an E3 ligase so the target gets ubiquitinated and destroyed. Unlike PROTACs, they do not necessarily have two distinct binding heads joined by a linker.

A famous group is the **IMiDs** (immunomodulatory imide drugs), including thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide. They bind the protein **cereblon (CRBN)**, a substrate receptor of the CRL4^CRBN E3 ligase. By changing cereblon's surface, they cause it to recognize new proteins called **neosubstrates**. Important examples are transcription factors IKZF1 (Ikaros) and IKZF3 (Aiolos), whose destruction contributes to activity against certain blood cancers.

Different glues can recruit different neosubstrates. Lenalidomide, for example, also promotes degradation of CK1α (casein kinase 1 alpha), especially relevant in a particular subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome. The details depend on cell type and compound.

The advantage of glues is their smaller size compared with many PROTACs, often aiding cell entry. The challenge is discovering exactly which proteins they bring together: effects can be surprising and unwanted. Also, the older drug thalidomide caused devastating fetal harm, a reason this drug class requires extremely strict safety controls in clinical use. Understanding glue-driven degradation helps scientists design safer and more selective molecules.
levels.college:
Molecular glues promote a protein–protein interaction through a compact ligand, typically by binding one partner and creating or stabilizing an interface for the other. In degradation, that interface recruits a neosubstrate to an E3 ligase, resulting in ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction. Glue-like mechanisms also exist outside degradation (e.g., some natural products stabilize immunophilin–target complexes); the phrase "molecular glue degrader" specifies the UPS outcome.

**IMiDs** are well-studied cereblon modulators. Thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide bind a tryptophan-rich pocket of CRBN, a substrate receptor in the CRL4^CRBN complex. The exposed drug surface recruits neosubstrates such as IKZF1 and IKZF3, whose depletion is linked to therapeutic effects in multiple myeloma. Lenalidomide also promotes degradation of CK1α in del(5q) myelodysplastic syndrome, illustrating how related molecules can recruit distinct targets.

Proteomic mapping is essential because small changes to the glue or the neosubstrate surface can alter the degrader's profile. Methods include time-resolved global proteomics with proteasome-rescue controls, proximity labeling, affinity purification and CRBN-loss genetics. Structural studies of E3–glue–neosubstrate complexes identify the interface driving selectivity.

IMiDs have complex immunomodulatory and anticancer effects beyond a simple one-target story. Historical thalidomide exposure caused severe birth defects; its clinical use now has rigorous risk-management programs. This is a mechanistic safety lesson: recruit an unintended developmental protein and a successful molecular glue can be harmful. Medicinal chemists seek new ligases and more selective glue scaffolds while testing broad neosubstrate profiles.
levels.phd:
Molecular glue degraders illustrate how induced interfaces generate emergent pharmacology. A low-molecular-weight ligand binds a pocket on one protein, reshaping its surface to favor a previously weak or absent interaction with another. The interface can be highly cooperative: many contacts are protein–protein, not protein–ligand. Consequently, the neosubstrate may not bind the free small molecule detectably yet still be recruited avidly to the ligase–glue complex.

Structural work on CRL4^CRBN–IMiD complexes identified a ligand-bound substrate receptor that recruits zinc-finger transcription factors IKZF1/3 through a defined degron. Small changes in the drug's exposed chemistry or in target surface residues alter recruitment. Other cereblon modulators engage additional neosubstrates, and species differences in cereblon or the neosubstrate can make animal toxicity models unreliable for human-specific degradation.

The field expanded beyond serendipitous IMiDs. Aryl sulfonamides such as indisulam recruit the splicing factor RBM39 to DCAF15, another E3 substrate receptor. Discovery approaches include phenotypic screening followed by proteomic target identification and chemoproteomic mapping of E3-bound compounds. Rational design remains harder than for PROTACs because a glue's target interface often emerges only in the assembled complex.

Mechanistic evidence should connect compound binding to the E3, neosubstrate recruitment, ubiquitination, proteasome-dependent depletion and downstream phenotype. Time-course proteomics can distinguish primary neosubstrates from later transcriptional consequences. Comparing dose–response, E3-null cells and proteasome rescue identifies true substrates. The thalidomide tragedy also makes embryo-developmental substrate profiling and species-specific biology important even when the intended indication is unrelated.

Glues may offer superior permeability to bifunctional degraders but poorer predictability of neosubstrate scope; there is no intrinsic guarantee of safety in either format.
levels.expert:
A team discovering a putative glue should resist naming the target from a single late proteomics time point. Many proteins fall downstream of stress or altered transcription. The direct neosubstrate is the one whose recruitment, ubiquitination and early proteasome-dependent depletion can be shown with orthogonal methods.

For cereblon glues, confirm compound binding to CRBN and loss of activity in CRBN-null cells. Use proteasome rescue and early global proteomics to list candidate neosubstrates, then validate binary versus ternary binding and solve structures where possible. Measure effects across human cell types because neosubstrate expression and E3 components vary. Critically, a safety panel should seek unintended developmental or immune-relevant substrates, not only the intended cancer target.

Compared with PROTACs, molecular glues are often smaller and more conventional in oral drug-like properties. But their compactness reduces the designer's direct control over target selection. A small modification may change which proteins are recruited without obvious changes in standard binding assays. A useful structure–degradation relationship therefore tracks proteome-wide depletion, not just one target's DC50.

IMiDs taught a sobering lesson: a treatment can deliver major benefit in tightly controlled settings while carrying profound harm if fetal exposure occurs. Their history does not invalidate the mechanism; it demands rigorous patient protections and neosubstrate testing. Newer glue programs should be judged by verified substrate profiles, tissue exposure and clinical evidence rather than the elegance of the proximity concept.

keyPoints: Molecular glue degraders create or stabilize an E3–neosubstrate interface.
IMiDs bind cereblon, recruiting IKZF1 and IKZF3 for degradation.
Lenalidomide can also recruit CK1α in del(5q) myelodysplastic syndrome.
Indisulam recruits RBM39 to DCAF15.
Small chemical changes can change substrate profile; proteomic safety checks are essential.

lessons.title: Degrader drug-likeness

levels.kid:
A tiny medicine can often slip through a cell's outer membrane. A big PROTAC has a harder trip. It carries two grabbing ends and a chain, so it may be bulky and have lots of sticky spots that love water. The cell membrane is more like oil, so some big watery molecules struggle to enter.

Scientists try different chains and shapes to help a degrader fold up and hide those sticky spots while crossing the wall. Then it can unfold inside the cell and grab its target and E3 helper. They also check whether the cell pumps it back out. A degrader that works beautifully in a test tube but never enters a real cell cannot remove the protein there.
levels.hs:
PROTACs promise new ways to remove proteins, but they are often unusually large molecules. A typical one joins two binding ligands with a linker, so its **molecular weight**, hydrogen-bonding groups and **polar surface area** often exceed Lipinski's Rule-of-Five guidelines for orally absorbed small molecules.

Why this matters:
- A cell membrane has a fatty interior. Very polar molecules may not cross it easily.
- **Efflux pumps** can send a degrader back out of the cell.
- Large molecules may dissolve poorly or be broken down before reaching the intended tissue.
- A compound can bind both target and E3 in a test tube but still fail in cells because it cannot get inside.

Chemists solve these problems by changing linker length, rigidity and polarity; reducing exposed hydrogen-bond donors; and using intramolecular hydrogen bonds that hide polar groups while the molecule crosses a membrane. This shape-changing property is sometimes called **chameleonicity**.

Not every degrader must be a pill: different routes of administration may be appropriate if exposure is a barrier, but each route requires its own safety and tissue-distribution work. The main rule is to measure what actually reaches cells and tissues, not assume that good purified-protein results will translate.

Molecular glues, being smaller, may have easier cell entry, but their selectivity can be harder to predict. No format wins every time.
levels.college:
Targeted protein degraders occupy **beyond-Rule-of-Five (bRo5)** chemical space. Bifunctional PROTACs typically have high molecular weight, topological polar surface area (TPSA), rotatable-bond counts and multiple hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors. These features reduce passive membrane permeability and sometimes oral bioavailability; they do not make useful systemic exposure impossible.

Structure–property levers:
- **Linker optimization**: shortening, rigidifying or reducing heteroatoms can improve permeability, but changes may disrupt ternary geometry.
- **Intramolecular hydrogen bonds (IMHBs)**: mask donors and acceptors in low-dielectric membrane-like conditions while allowing more open aqueous conformations. This environmental conformational change is chameleonicity.
- **Macrocyclization** can preorganize a useful conformation and alter exposed polarity, though chemistry becomes harder.
- **E3 recruiter selection** changes polarity and metabolic stability; CRBN and VHL ligands have different profiles.

Measurements should separate passive permeability (PAMPA), cellular permeability and efflux (Caco-2 or MDCK), intracellular unbound concentration, metabolic stability, plasma protein binding and tissue exposure. A total tissue concentration may not reflect free intracellular compound available for ternary assembly.

Drug-like performance also depends on pharmacodynamics. If a target stays depleted after a degrader leaves, sustained exposure may not be necessary; if target synthesis is rapid, brief exposure may fail. The PK/PD relationship is more complex than inhibitor occupancy because degradation and protein resynthesis have their own kinetics.

Molecular glues are often smaller and may navigate conventional drug-like space more readily, but their unpredictable neosubstrate recruitment can shift the challenge from permeability to selectivity.
levels.phd:
bRo5 degrader optimization requires moving beyond simple two-dimensional property filters. TPSA computed from structure is not the same as the solvent-exposed polar surface area of a folded conformation. In a low-dielectric environment, a PROTAC may form IMHBs and bury donors, crossing membranes more effectively than static descriptors predict; in water it may reopen. Ensemble-based exposed-polarity calculations and NMR or crystallographic evidence can probe this behavior.

Permeability is not one number. PAMPA measures passive diffusion without transporters; Caco-2/MDCK assays incorporate efflux; cellular accumulation measures total compound, not unbound cytosolic concentration. Lysosomal trapping and membrane partitioning can inflate total uptake while lowering free cytosolic drug. Measuring intracellular unbound fraction and target engagement helps distinguish these mechanisms.

Optimization is intrinsically multiparameter. A change that improves permeability by removing a linker oxygen may worsen ternary cooperativity or solubility. Rigidification can lower entropic penalties for complex formation yet reduce adaptable folding. Macrocycles may improve exposed polarity in a favorable conformer but suffer difficult synthesis or poor solubility. There is no monotonic descriptor that captures this space.

PK/PD models of degradation incorporate tissue-specific unbound drug, ternary formation, ubiquitination rate, proteasomal clearance and target synthesis. Metrics such as DC50 and Dmax shift with E3 expression, target copy number and cell type, so translating in-vitro depletion to an organ requires exposure-adjusted mechanistic modeling. Recovery after washout provides an empirical check on target resynthesis.

Clinical progress with bifunctional degraders shows that bRo5 chemistry need not doom an oral candidate, but published clinical results should be interpreted for the specific molecule and indication rather than as a guarantee for the whole format.
levels.expert:
For degrader programs, beautiful cellular DC50 data are only the opening bid. The development question is whether unbound compound reaches enough target cells for long enough, while sparing tissues where E3-mediated degradation would be harmful.

Design teams run parallel chemistry tracks: linkers with different polarity and rigidity, target-binding vectors and E3-recruiting motifs. They measure ternary potency and cellular depletion alongside passive permeability, efflux, solubility, microsomal stability and exposure. Optimizing one number in isolation rarely works; a more permeable analogue that loses productive ternary geometry is not an advance.

Common traps:
- High total intracellular concentration mistaken for high free cytosolic concentration when compound is trapped in organelles or membranes.
- A strong purified-protein ternary signal mistaken for cellular efficacy despite efflux.
- Plasma exposure mistaken for brain exposure; blood–brain barrier entry is especially demanding for large polar degraders.
- Protein loss in one engineered cell line generalized to tissues with different E3 expression or target turnover.

At a candidate review, compare free tissue exposure with a cellular degradation concentration–response and its hook region. Measure target recovery after compound clears. Use disease-relevant cells to confirm E3 expression, selectivity and functional response. If oral exposure fails, another route may be worth exploring, but only if it matches the clinical need and distribution profile.

The senior judgment is a balance of chemistry, cell biology and patient context: removal of the right protein in the right tissue matters more than a record-setting DC50 in an easy cell line.

keyPoints: Large, polar bifunctional degraders often sit beyond Rule-of-Five space.
Linker optimization and intramolecular H-bonds can improve permeability.
PAMPA measures passive diffusion; cellular assays reveal efflux and accumulation.
Total cellular or tissue drug does not equal unbound cytosolic concentration.
Tissue E3 expression, target turnover and exposure shape real pharmacodynamics.
